TASK: CHECK EACH SENTENCE AGAINST THE CLAIMS

You are an adversarial fact checker. Your job is to find every sentence below that says something the CLAIMS do not support. Do not pass a sentence to be agreeable and do not fail one to look diligent. A sentence may read as confident or well written; that is evidence about its writer, not about the claims.

Label every sentence with exactly one of:
- "supported": every factual part of the sentence (each number, each name, each count, each comparison, each cause, each "most", "all", "only" or "none") is stated by one or more of the claims, or follows from them directly with no new number. Give the ids of the claims that together support it.
- "unsupported": any factual part is not stated by the claims, contradicts them, changes a number, drops a qualification a claim carries ("at most", "a bound", "notional", "not established", "candidate"), or states a number no claim states. Say which part, in the reason.
- "no_factual_content": the sentence states nothing that could be true or false about the world: a transition, a statement of what the section will do, a definition of a word the report uses.

The NAMES table maps a code in a claim to the name a sentence uses; a sentence that uses the name is read as if it used the code. A sentence that names a statistical body is checked against the claims for that body.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per sentence, in order, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
[{"sentence_id": "S1", "label": "supported", "claim_ids": ["CL-035"], "reason": "one short sentence"}]

NAMES
A6: the check for structured markup (schema.org/Dataset (or DCAT/Croissant) markup valid on product pages)
A7: the check for stable identifiers (Persistent URLs/DOIs for products and vintages)
A8: the check for timeliness of surface (Release date machine-readable; latest-vintage pointer resolvable)
B2: the check for definitions surface (Concept/term definitions published, versioned, linked from variables)
B3: the check for methodology legibility (Methodology docs in structured text (not PDF-only); summarizable by retrieval)
B5: the check for semantic consistency (Same concept ⇒ same identifier across products/vintages)
C5: the check for readiness metrics baseline (Product scored against published AI-data-readiness metrics)
D1: the check for license clarity (Explicit machine-readable license/terms on product and API)
D2: the check for reuse permissions for ai (Terms address model training/retrieval use explicitly)
F2: the check for contract stability (API/schema changes are versioned; breaking changes announced with deprecation windows; compatibility checked mechanically)
F3: the check for regression on vintage transition (Time-series identifiers, geography codes, and endpoints survive a new vintage or a crosswalk is published; tested per release)
F4: the check for change legibility (Machine-readable changelog per release (what changed, why, revision class); webhooks/push for high-frequency products)
F6: the check for release authenticity (Signed releases / provenance attestations so downstream copies are traceable to the authoritative artifact (SLSA-class, adapted))
G3: the check for classification/vintage identity (Stable series IDs; machine-readable crosswalks when classifications or geographies change (industry codes, boundary revisions))

[CL-079] (prior_art) A federal agency's flagship data product must be listed in its `data.json`.
    note: The status rests on the obligation covering every data asset, of which a flagship product is one. The statute and the guidance state the obligation for all data assets in the agency's possession; neither names flagship products. M-13-13 and the Project Open Data schema were not searched on the web: the current obligation (M-25-05, which names DCAT-US 3.0 as the inventory schema) is in the corpus, and the schema documents dcat-us-1-1-schema and dcat-us-3-overview are admitted.
    evidence: Evidence Act Title II, the amended 44 U.S.C. § 3511(a)(1), PDF p. 10 | quote: "develop and maintain a comprehensive data inventory that accounts for all data assets" | note: fss-policy-kg holds the same obligation: Obligation d7b0b83364ef4c66aa6e4718e267ca83 (source_doc evidence_act_2018) and 2346470a44d0415e855ad23ce5814085 (source_doc pra_1995_uslm).
    evidence: OMB M-25-05, comprehensive data inventories, (iii) Public Dissemination, PDF p. 10 | quote: "host it publicly on the agency’s website at the address: www.[agency].gov/data.json" | note: fss-policy-kg: Obligation 069f7c3081b64954b785c34ca1be3c22 (source_doc m_25_05); the inventory requirement itself is Obligation 7bf4bc7524e34df9bcdccac539f39ed3 (m_25_05, PDF p. 7: data assets held by more than one agency are 'required to be listed independently by each agency').

SENTENCES
S1: With those limits stated, the report turns to what an agency can do, and for the Census Bureau every prescribed fix that the claims name sits in the notional hours effort band and carries no cost.
S2: Under equal weights, each fix can raise the bureau's hierarchical score by at most a stated amount, which is the gain if every failing result on the matching indicator passed; because no weighting is asserted, each amount is a bound and not a value.
S3: The largest of these amounts comes from the changelog, where carrying a revision class on every entry addresses the check for change legibility and can add at most 0.25.
S4: Two pairs of fixes address the conditions under which a machine may reuse the bureau's data.
S5: The first pair publishes a machine-readable licence and states that licence as an identifier rather than as a sentence, and both serve the check for license clarity with at most 0.125 each.
S6: The second pair declares the terms for AI training and AI input in robots.txt and keeps to the categories and values that the Content Signals Policy defines, and both serve the check for reuse permissions for AI, again with at most 0.125 each.
S7: The remaining fixes concern how the bureau explains its concepts and describes its data to a machine.
S8: Three of them serve the test, discussed in the previous section, of whether concept definitions are published and linked from variables: publishing the concept definitions as schema.org defined terms, giving each linked one a code, a set and a definition, and linking them from the variables, each with a ceiling of 0.083.
S9: The same ceiling of 0.083 applies to naming the set that each code belongs to, which serves the check for semantic consistency, and to linking the methodology from the product page, which serves the test for methodology legibility.
S10: Fixes to the markup on that page carry a ceiling of at most 0.036 each, and embedding JSON-LD that describes the data, typing the existing markup as a Dataset, and making that markup conform to the profile it declares all address the test for structured markup.
S11: Publishing a release date and declaring the vintage in the markup, not only in a file header, address the test for timeliness of surface under that same limit.
S12: Tying each measured result to a prescribed fix is not new, because outside-in measurement of an organization's published surface, with a remediation step named for each result, is an existing pattern in tools such as Lighthouse and OpenSSF Scorecard.
S13: The difference that the documentation read for this report shows is the effort band, because every fix prescribed here carries a notional one, whereas none of the results in that documentation carries an effort estimate.
S14: However, that absence is noted over the sources read and is not established for the literature as a whole, so it marks a difference from the tools examined rather than a finding of novelty.
S15: What the framework measures next depends on what blocks each indicator that still lacks a measured verdict.
S16: Of the 25 such indicators, 11 wait on a standard, 7 on the agency's cooperation, 6 on open tooling, 0 on funding, and 1 is not blocked.
S17: The next measurements therefore take up the indicators that can be read from outside with public tools and no agency action.
S18: For example, the Wayback CDX server can supply the evidence for the indicators of stable identifiers and of regression on vintage transition, AIDRIN can supply it for the readiness metrics baseline, and the SLSA verifier can supply it for release authenticity.
S19: The indicator for contract stability compares two releases with oasdiff, so it must wait for a second scan.
S20: The check for classification/vintage identity is also within reach, because a standard already admitted names the artifact it would read, and the only missing piece is a collector that this project would write.
S21: Each of these indicators is to be measured before the summary is drafted, and none of them requires anything from the agency.
